Writing Tips: The Real Conditional in Expository Writing
The Present Real Conditional is used to talk about what you normally do in situations that are real or likely to happen.
You use the Present Real Conditional in expository writing to convey the result or outcome of a condition. The result is always true or likely to happen.

Structure:
If/When ... Simple Present ... , ... Simple Present ...
... Simple Present ... if/when ... Simple Present ....
If and when are usually interchangeable. However, if suggests that something happens less frequently. When suggests that something happens more regularly.
Read the following examples of Real Conditional in expository writing.
Currently, if you download music illegally, there are very few consequences.
These same people believe that if an artist still retains his or her own electronic copy of their work, it is not theft.
Essentially, artists feel that if someone downloads a song it  is the same as stealing someone's unique invention.
If someone steals your personal property, it is illegal.
Writing Tips: Common Mistakes with Future Perfect Simple and Continuous

You use the Future Perfect Simple and the Future Perfect Continuous to talk about future actions that will be completed at a moment in the future, or about actions that will be in progress at a time later than now.
The Future Perfect tense shows that an action will have been completed at some point in the future. This tense is formed with will + have + the past participle of the verb.

There are two different forms of Future Perfect: will have done and be going to have done.
Future Perfect forms are usually interchangeable.

Structure:
will have + past participle, or
am/is/are + going to have + past participle
The Future Perfect Continuous refers to an unfinished action or event that will be in progress at a time later than now.
There are two forms of Future Perfect Continuous: will have been doing and going to have been doing.

Have you ever downloaded music illegally? Does digital media count as property?
As of next year, the downloading of music will have been operating for over two decades.

Downloading has been a constant source of frustration for the music industry. In recent years, the Internet has opened up questionable doors in the field of ethics and the ability to download music has been cause for headaches for artists.  Essentially, they believe that individuals are stealing from them each time one of their songs is illegally downloaded. Currently, if you download music illegally, there are very few consequences. Some camps argue that knowledge should be free and that artists' works fall under that category. These same people believe that if an artist still retains his or her own electronic copy of their work, it is not theft.

However, many believe that this justification is baseless and illegal. They feel that there needs to be a separation between what are ideas, which are freely available, and the stealing of a unique medium through which it is expressed. Essentially, artists feel that if someone downloads a song it is the same as stealing someone's unique invention. According to the definition of the term, theft simply refers to the act of taking what is not ours. Whether the artist still owns a copy is then inconsequential.
Hopefully, laws will have strengthened in the next couple years and artists will have received the royalties that they are currently missing out on.
